utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you are to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello to everyone. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jordan. We will continue with what we had started yesterday. If you remember, we ended the day on a photograph, a photograph that had been published in the Providence Journal in November 1994.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we need to display it. So after coming to The Hague on January 18, 2007, in view of your testimony here, you talked to the Prosecutor. Do you remember talking to the Prosecutor on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with the Prosecutor on Saturday and Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I have the notes and the report on this talk you had, and about this incident that occurred on November 18, 1994, you said that: [In English] "Dzenana and her son were walking towards the town when they were shot from the right from Serb positions." [Interpretation] Do you remember having said this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having conveyed that my personnel's report to me was that they had been shot from the right, from the Serb positions. Again, I wasn't there so I was only saying what my personnel on the scene had told me what they thought happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, like the entire incident actually was relayed by a third party to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, several third parties. Again, I was not present, only my personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So for the purposes of my cross-examination, I will show you a document that was tendered by the Prosecutor and that relates to this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my case manager please call up document P107.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a medical report, medical document. It's a physician that actually drafted this, and he testified here and he certified that these documents were authentic, the documents that are in this affidavit. Do you see on number 9 in that chart -- maybe read the description that we have here, on number 9.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The patient had wounds caused by bullet in the part of abdominal." That's number 9 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But then before that there is the description. The description, that's the previous column. Could you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be number 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not number 8 but this column "Description," the column that's right before the one that you read.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. "Health record certificate issued by the medical centre for Dzenana Sokolovic, University Medical Centre, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could move on to the next page now, please, on the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you see number 10?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Health record certificate issued by medical centre for Dzenana Sokolovic, University Medical Centre, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, may I just ask, how much more time would you be spending on your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to be extremely brief, as far as possible, of course. I will finish with this incident and then I will move to another topic which would take me about ten minutes, and I need a map. And then there are a few questions I would like to ask to the witness that are closely linked to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question. You have given me a narration but not an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll give you 45 minutes, if you need that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, do you remember that name, Dzenana Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned it when -- oh, at least we can see that in the report on the talks you had with the Prosecutor. [In English] "Men who worked for him as firemen were present in front of the museum when Dzenana Sokolovic and her son were shot."

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of Dzenana Sokolovic. I don't remember talking to her. Maybe I just knew her as a doctor or something. It just doesn't seem familiar to me. I've never seen these documents before. We didn't have anything to do with the administration. We picked up casualties, dropped them at the hospital, and that was the end of our end of it. This is administrative stuff that I would have had nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear. Dzenana Sokolovic was not a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It's the victim, the victim of this -- the mother of the kid that you talked about, you know, in your declaration, in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often did not know the names of folks, ma'am. I could have very well given a description of an incident and not known the folks' names.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So in that case, let's move to the evidence we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need document D19; the 65 ter number is 1484. Could we please have that on the screen. If we could please have page 10 of this document. In the Prosecution's file, this document is separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We have the document here on the screen. So this is for Dzenana Sokolovic, who is the mother of that child we talked about yesterday. On the screen, in the middle of the document, we have a passage starting with "Entry point ..." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this line of questioning. We tried to present these medical records to a doctor and have him interpret them and the Defence objected and the objection was sustained by the Trial Chamber. Now the Defence is trying to present medical records to somebody who, number 1, was not at the scene himself, number 2, had nothing to do with the medical treatment of this patient, and, number 3, is not a doctor. And so to cross-examine him with medical records under those circumstances seems to me to be far afield and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We sustain the objection. Move on, Ms. Isailovic, to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Could my case manager please call up map P194, 65 ter number 2927.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Jordan, could you please take your statement. I believe it's lying in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And look at paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the court officer please zoom in on the map so that we can have the Miljacka right in the middle of the map, the river Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, yesterday you were talking about the army of Republika Srpska, but you said "the people in the hills." That's the way you referred to them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I used that term because I didn't particularly want to label a whole people. I don't know anybody in Belgrade, but, you know, I just kept the whole thing local. That was the issue to us. So I didn't use the term "Serb"; I tried to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on paragraph 26, you say: [In English] "... from the heights they could drop a round anywhere." [Interpretation] Do you see that? It's on the fourth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't catch what -- something got mixed up in the translation. I couldn't catch which line was being read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon me, there was a glitch in the transmission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the line being referred to? Is it the fourth line?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It starts on the third line. It starts with "In spite ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [In English]"In spite of random shells landing anywhere in the town ..." [Interpretation] Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have a map on the screen. Just ignore what is written on the map, except for the basic geographical concepts. Can you find your way on this map, Mr. Jordan? Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. The general region is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the usher please come and help you with the electronic pen. We're going to spend some time on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, could you draw a line along the Miljacka, the river that runs through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you mentioned Mount Trebevic several times. Could you locate this on this map, Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contour lines aren't quite as visible as they could be, but Trebevic was a height to the south, if I remember right. I remember it in general terms, Trebevic being to the south, Zuc to the north, and Mojmilo hill down near Dobrinja. I mean, if the map was a smaller scale I'm sure I could find it; but anything else is just a random guess after 11 years. I remember it being to the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever climb or go up Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure we were on it at one time or another, heading to Pale or somewhere else. We were up and down most of the hills to a degree, as long as there were population centres near them or anything that could burn that we could put out. We would have to go around Zuc on occasion to get to Vogosca auto plant when there were fires there, and up and down the different hills within BiH territory to get to fires. And to get to fire on the BSA side, we generally would have to go around the airport, through Lukavica. The bridge over there was only opened intermittently, so we couldn't always access that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You know the city well, so can you tell us what area, what neighbourhood, of Sarajevo was located at the foot of Mount Trebevic? Maybe that might help to locate Trebevic on the map. So what neighbourhood was at its foot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived mostly in Skenderija and they'd point up the hill, I believe it was towards Trebevic, which would also make it above Grbavica. I don't know what the area above Bistrik was called. That was also high ground. And then, like I say, across the river to the north, there was Zuc, which was BiH-held. The other side was --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let's just stick to Trebevic for the moment, if possible. Do you know that Trebevic has several peaks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the hills around Sarajevo had -- most of the hills anywhere have more than one peak. There's the highest part and then there's what's called the military crest, and it's just -- like I say, this is what maps are for, not memory. We don't -- you know, to be precise, you have to have the map in front of you. I wouldn't venture to guess. That's why we make maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you knew, then, that the peaks at Trebevic were Debelo Brdo. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sitting here remembering that now. No, ma'am. Again, that's why I would need a more detailed map. I probably knew it at the time, but again, that's when I was seeing it and it was a threat to myself and my personnel every day. You know, I knew the streets in Beirut pretty well; I wouldn't venture to say I knew them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The peak called Colina Kapa, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What about Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We identified things mainly by sights or -- you're asking me to use a pen here, but when we made maps for my personnel's use, we basically used a brush and said, "This is an area to avoid, this is an area to avoid" and didn't break it down to the name of a peak or a grid coordinate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What about Grad?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lots of Grads in Sarajevo. Novi Grad. "Grad" was kind of a generic term, if I remember right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you don't recall Grad as being one of the peaks in Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jordan, I can only infer from this that you don't -- you weren't too familiar with the hills around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the witness has been clear in his answer about what he might remember now versus what you knew then and how he knew it. So to characterise his testimony like that I think is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that counsel said? She said she can only infer from this that he wasn't too familiar with the hills around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, which I think misstates his evidence, because he has been clear -- without repeating what he's said, he's been, I think, clear about what he knew at the time versus what he knows today and how he knew things at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the witness can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I knew what I needed to know at the time. I didn't speak the language fluently. I knew my way around on the ground very well. This was acknowledged by the UN who often asked us to guide new troops in over Igman mountain. The fact is, the only time the US embassy ever brought its own people over the mountain, unescorted by us, they lost people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move to Mount Zuc, then. You mentioned Zuc earlier. Do you remember where Zuc was located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right across from where we built the station. It had that large radio tower on top. It was a target. Just a big radio tower on the hill to the north, more or less in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So for you, this radio antenna or TV antenna was located on Zuc?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a big antenna up there on the mountain, if I remember right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go up Mount Zuc?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One of my personnel did once and he was fired for that, because we had no business up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know of a neighbourhood in Sarajevo called Vogosca? That would be located at the foot of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, ma'am, if you say so. I remember some areas more distinctly than others because of them having small fire stations in them. But, again, it's 11 years ago. I don't remember all the neighbourhoods like I did when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jordan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, it doesn't appear to me that you're getting anywhere with this line of questioning. The witness has clearly said what he knows and what he doesn't know. So you must decide whether -- how much longer you will spend in cross-examination. I'd said 45 minutes, and that's 45 minutes from the beginning of this session, but it appears to me that you may have exhausted your questions. Do you have other pertinent questions to ask of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was a comment I wanted to make. The witness made this statement on August 22nd, 23rd, and 24th, 2006. It's a very detailed statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the date of the statement, Mr. Witness, August 2006? You agree with the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, if you say so. I don't remember the dates I was here exactly, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could I infer from this that everything you say in this statement is quite broad and according to your recollection, which wasn't any better than it is today just a year after this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question, ma'am. I knew the city very specifically when I was there. I think I probably still know more about it than most folks who haven't been there now. The fact that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not challenging this; of course not. We saw the video clip; we saw that you were on site. What I'm challenging here in this courtroom is, well, maybe the authenticity of your statement, the truth of the statement, because it dates back eight months. You made this statement eight months ago, and there's a lot of details in the statement. I have 15 more minutes and I will ask a few questions about the statement in these 15 minutes. But there are 50 paragraphs to your statement. You go into detail. And today you're telling us that your recollection is vague --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- which is normal because so much time has elapsed since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you must put a question to the witness instead of making a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think counsel just misstated the evidence. The witness has not said his recollection is very vague. He has said with respect to pointing things out on a map, locations, only with respect to that has he -- did he say that today it's difficult for him to remember exactly where things were and to point them out on a map. But he has not said as a general matter that his recollection is vague. So I think that counsel has misstated the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a fine distinction, but I think it is well founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed with my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that your recollections today do not enable you to talk about what happened to you in detail when you were a fireman in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would respectfully disagree with that. I remember very well what happened to me over two and a half years of doing fire and rescue work in Sarajevo. The authenticity and truthfulness of anything I had to say is authentic and truthful in my own mind, and anyone else can decide in their own mind if I cannot answer a pop quiz of where things are -- that I had nothing to do with, are on a map, if I did not know Sarajevo. That's up to them, if they want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, this is nothing personal against you. You do what you can. So let's move on to paragraph 22 of your statement. I would like to spend some time talking about the weapons that were used in Sarajevo at the time. Can we agree that you used a sniper when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rifle that myself and my personnel carried in Sarajevo was a standard issue rifle in the US, in the late 1950s, early 1960s and even into the 1970s. It was only a sniper rifle if one put a scope on it. I did not always do that. Sometimes I just used it in its normal battle configuration. But yes, I used a sniper rifle in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I understand, you weren't a member of UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR were the sole people entitled to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that they had an exclusivity on the carriage of weapons. I understood that they were called United Nations Protection Forces and did not do that job, which was why I wound up carrying a weapon or I wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, we have heard a number of UN military observers here, and according to their statements, we know that they were not entitled to carry weapons, which was not very convenient for them. Did you know that, that the UN military observers were not armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that UN military observers were traditionally not armed. I know some, on occasion, did carry handguns, but that is actually neither here nor there. Their policy was to not be armed. That's their call. That has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you were a fire-fighter, you and your friends. You, nonetheless, were carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our mission, as has always been stated, was to assist, improve and protect. On the protect end, we were basically operating in an advanced form of, say, fire marshalls who are armed and arrest arsonists who are dangerous felons, which in this case, in Sarajevo, was a very advanced version of the armed, dangerous felon who was also an arsonist. We just considered it a major extrapolation of one element of fire-fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I live in France. I have never seen armed fire-fighters, but maybe this is a broad view of things and a broad view of what a fire-fighter is. From what I understand, you reckoned you were something like a sheriff or a fire marshall. This is the word I heard in the French translation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sheriff" would probably be incorrect. "Fire marshall" would be correct. We did not arrest folks, per se, because we often could not access the folks who were assaulting firemen, which is a crime in just about any country, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, can we agree and say that in Sarajevo at the time, it was very difficult to control who was carrying arms and who wasn't?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree. The locals on both sides were very circumspect about who carried arms. A lot of citizens on both sides carried handguns for protection, but the carriage of military arms was, in general, restricted to military or paramilitary personnel on both sides. Both sides frowned on somebody just running around with a gun unless they were part of some unit or another. So while it may look quite loose to outsider, it as quite structured, actually, by local standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just seek a clarification, Mr. Jordan. Did you have the power to arrest arsonists or anybody who was committing a misdemeanour in relation to the cause of a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That issue actually never came up, sir. We talked about it a lot. But I will say that if somebody assaulted one of my firemen and we could detain the person, I would do it, the same way that I tried to detain a group of men who decided to rob everybody on the train coming into Paddington Station a month ago. I mean, that's what a citizen does. You maintain civil order even if you're not in uniform. So, yes, I would. It just didn't come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraphs 47 and 48, if you could kindly turn to those paragraphs in your statement. If you could have a look at this, please. In your statement you talk about tourist shooters. After that, you talk about burgermeisters who would pay money to go to Sarajevo to shoot people from the Serb side. Mr. Jordan, do you remember having said that in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- in August of last year? And could you tell us where you got this information from at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had witnessed on more than one occasion personnel who did not appear to me to be locals by their dress, by the weapons they carried, by the way they were being handled, i.e., guided around by the locals. I saw this in Sarajevo on a number of occasions. Some of my other personnel had seen it in the Mostar area. The term "burgermeisters" is a slang term that refers to the fact that Croatia, being allied, friendly, i.e., Germany, that's where the tourists came from on that side. Up by us, kind of hard to get a tourist into Sarajevo to shoot uphill, so the tourists shot downhill.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you established a visual distinction between the locals and the foreigners in Sarajevo. This is what I can conclude on the basis of your statement. Is this true? Did you actually establish this distinction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can assume from my statement that I am a trained observer and can tell when one guy, who is obviously not familiar with an area, is being led, literally almost by the hand, around an area by people who are familiar it. This is where the term "tourist shooter" came from. The guy was not from the neighbourhood. He did not carry arms that were typical of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. You saw these people doing the job.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I never saw one of these tourist shooters take a shot. I just saw them being handled and moved around known sniper positions. I never actually saw one take a shot. But, again, it was clearly obvious that the person being led by men who were familiar with the ground was completely unfamiliar with the ground, and his manner of dress and the weapons they carried led me to believe they were tourist shooters. It was an expression that I ran into for the first time in Beirut where we saw the same thing happening around the green line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. How were these tourist shooters dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that they wore civilian/military combination-type clothing, but mostly it was the weapon. Anyone can go to a surplus store and outfit himself to look like anybody else's army. But the locals carried certain weapons, and when a guy shows up with a weapon that looks more like he ought to be hunting boar in the Black Forest than in urban combat in the Balkans, you know, when you see him being handled and you can obviously tell he is a novice at moving around rubble, you know, if it walks like a duck, talks like a duck, it's a duck.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Just one last question. Where did you see these people walking around with their weapons? In which neighbourhood of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions I saw individuals that fit that profile while I was visiting the Serb firemen in Grbavica, and on a couple of other occasions I saw them in different areas on BSA territory from various over-watch positions that I would take up to maintain over-watch of my fire-fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We are still talking about the same subject. Let's turn to paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you must be bringing your examination to a close now. We have been more than generous with the time allocated to you, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall put my question straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had time to look at your statement, Mr. Jordan? Amongst other things, you mentioned targeting here and you say that if a family was walking, it was always the youngest. In a crowd of girls, it seems that the most attractive would be shot. My question is the following: According to you, what selection criteria did the shooters have? Why was it that they chose the most attractive girls?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: God only knows, ma'am. With reference to killing of children, we responded over the years to a number of scenes where one member of a family, in the course of going about their business, was shot. We very often noticed that it was the youngest. One thing a person is taught as a military sniper is killing is not necessarily the end result; destruction is the end result. You kill a man, it's over. You wound a man, four have to carry him out. When you're targeting civilians like this, particularly families who may or may not be Muslim, shooting the child has the effect of literally disemboweling the whole family. In the more devout Muslim families, some of which existed in Sarajevo, even if a round came out of nowhere and killed your son, it would have the effect of gutting the family. The man would -- one of the worst insults you can give somebody in Sarajevo is, "You are not a man." If somebody kills your child, even if they do it from 800 metres away with a rifle, you have not defended your family, you are not a man. That one shot has gutted that family. They are all completely affected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordan. But do you remember a specific example of this, where somebody was shooting at a crowd of people but where the most attractive girl was shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, on more than one occasion I remember that kind of thing. We just -- I don't know how -- I don't know how to describe two years of seeing these things over and over again, and I can't remember all the dates and things like that. This was just daily life in Sarajevo for two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the cross-examination, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, you told us that you did not have a licence to carry your weapon and that you had no formal, legal authority to arrest people by virtue of your business in Sarajevo. I'm not going to go into that, but I just want to be sure that I have understood this was, in fact, the case.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian government forces gave me a gun permit. I asked the folks over in Lukavica if they wanted me to carry one, too, because they knew full well that I was armed. They told me, "Don't wore about it," so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well, thanks. Now, my question was to know, then, whether you ever used your weapon. Did you ever at any occasion shoot at somebody who attacked you or your people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How many times, and under which conditions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have to be a very overt threat or attack on my personnel. We didn't do punitive; we didn't do preemptive. We only dealt with active threats. I have, after the war, lectured extensively at the US Marine Warfighting Laboratory, in Quantico, and at the US Naval War College, in Newport, Rhode Island, on not killing snipers in these situations. I guess if I wanted to make a name for myself, it was a target-rich environment and I could have done that. But in a local environment, these kinds of urban peacekeeping/civilian war type of environments, when a foreign group comes in, you do not want to make yourself the focus of violence. Going after the snipers specifically would have done that to us. There were plenty of capable of men who could have ended our antics in short order. What we did was drive them off. If I saw a position that was firing on my personnel, I would basically engage it as close as I could, without specifically going for a body shot. Most of the snipers lacked -- the kind of snipers who shoot women and children lack intestinal fortitude. They aren't going to stay up under countersniper fire, which is basically what we did, countersniping work. I am sure that on a number of occasions somebody probably died as a result of my actions. It would be intellectually dishonest to say otherwise. But most of the time, you drop enough bricks on a guy's head, he leaves. He's out there to kill -- he's out there to kill and leave and not do it up against any resistance. This was typical among the snipers on both sides. I didn't find them particularly effective, particularly skilled, or particularly determined, which is probably the only reason we got away with what we did without being targeted by each side. We drove off -- we drove off cowards, and it wasn't that hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us just an impression how many times during your two and a half years in Sarajevo you, yourself, actually used your weapon; and in addition to that, how many times, just as a general estimate, did any of your folks use their weapons? To give the Bench an impression of how often was fire resistance or firing -- scaring off, as you say, used by the GOFRS.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The one thing I would like to point out is that the casualties on the Bosnian government fire-fighting side when we arrived were almost 20 per cent; approximately 15 killed and 55 wounded out of 300. I don't know the casualties on the BSA side. They said that was a military secret. That's fine. I do know their men took casualties, too. Because of the lack of aggression against the BSA fire-fighters I can't really say we protected them. They basically protected themselves. On the Sarajevo side, they did not lose a plan at a fire to violence after we arrived and instituted this programme after September 1993. They didn't lose anybody. Their casualties dropped to zero. People were still shot and killed in the streets all the way up to the end of the war. No Sarajevo fireman was killed after we arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. But can you give me an indication of the number of shots that was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fired hundreds of shots, sir. Hundreds. It would be a lie to say anything other than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And your people did the same.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on scores of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And your people did the same.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all my people were qualified. A number of my personnel, in addition to being firemen and medics, were qualified to use that. It wasn't across the board. Several of our personnel would not carry arms at all. That was fine, because it wasn't our primary duty; it was not something I insisted that everybody be able to do. Other than be familiar with weapons so as to -- in fighting fires in the Balkans, it's a lot like America; it's a gun culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you fight a fire in a building, you may come across weapons. You have to clear them and get them out of the way. You have to be able to handle them safely. So everybody took what we call dissimilar weapons courses so they just wouldn't get hurt by them in the course of getting them out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. When you were assisting in fire-fighting on the Serb-held territory, were you ever in a position where you had to scare off a sniper on the Muslim side, on the Bosnian Muslim side, the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will admit to a certain amount of childishness at this point. There was one time where somebody fired a couple of very random rounds at us and I think he got two or three rounds back and that was the end of it. They didn't really -- the violence threshold in Sarajevo was basically shovelled downhill and spooned uphill, if I could explain it that way, and there were reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, I have a question. Regarding the incident which took place in November 1994, during which the son was killed and the mother wounded. I can read in your statement, paragraph 12, you said: "There was a Newsweek article about that incident which was erroneous in that it said that there were two shots; one which killed the boy and one which wounded the mother. In actuality, there was one well-aimed shot which hit them both." My question is: Do you have any foundation to affirm what you are saying, that there was one shot and not two?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have the reports of my personnel which I consider reliable, who saw a mother and son go down at the same time as a result of one shot. The article I referred to was, to me, symptomatic of the problem in the whole conflict. You had folks who -- it wasn't bad enough that some child got shot in the head. Some reporter had to somehow extrapolate the terror. It was the other side of -- there were people who said that the BiH were constantly shelling themselves; there were people who said the Serbs are particularly cruel and first they shot the boy and then they shot the mother. There was plenty of this crap on both sides. And that was an element of the war. It bothered me that an American publication with the esteem of Newsweek would give the whole back page of their paper to a reporter from one side of the conflict or another who had an agenda, because I thought the extrapolation of an existing horror was, in itself, intellectually dishonest and didn't help the problem for anybody. It pissed me off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, did your group go into Sarajevo on the basis of agreement with the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I went pretty naive. It took a couple of weeks to figure out what the score was there. I went to Sarajevo to help a fire department based on what I saw in the media. The media didn't say there were two fire departments that needed help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, what I'm trying to find out is, was there anything that set out the terms of your operation, how you would operate in the work that you were doing, or were you just left to do as you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were given a pretty free hand. The BSA side was always pretty fair with us. I never had a problem on their territory. The Bosnian side was very fragmented. The higher -- I shouldn't even say "higher." One section of the Bosnian government approved of our actions and didn't mind that we also helped the Bosnian Serb firemen. Then there were elements on the BiH side who said, "You're helping our enemies," which is why we got so much more movement problems on BiH territory than we did on BSA. Again, that goes back to command and control. The BSA had it; Bosnians didn't know who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Jordan, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Witness W-28 who has protective measures of face distortion and pseudonym. This witness is a 92 ter witness, and what I plan to do is put in his statements, ask a few background questions, put in a few documents, and then bring it to a close, a rapid close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. As you know, you have been granted protective measures of face distortion and we will be using a pseudonym instead of your real name. So to begin the proceedings, I'm going to ask the usher to show you a document and I'm just going to ask if you can confirm that this is in fact your name on the document. Please don't read it out. Just say yes or no, whether it's your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If that can be shown to Defence counsel and then to the Bench and entered into evidence under seal, please. And the pseudonym for the witness is W-28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P274 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going to show you two statements which you made, and the copies I have you'll see there's one on 22nd February 1996 and one on 11 March 1997, and there's both the English and the B/C/S with each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have copies of these statements for the Bench and for Defence counsel, if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you give these two statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review them before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are they true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you were to be asked about these topics today that are contained in the statements, is it the evidence that you would give here in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could these two statements be entered into evidence under seal. Just for the benefit of the registrar, the statement of 22 February 1996 has 65 ter number 2867, and 11 March 1997 has 65 ter number 2973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P275 and Exhibit P276 respectively, both under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02867, the statement of 22 February 1996, will be P275, and the next, 65 ter number 02973, the statement of 11 March 1997, will be P276, both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- in 1994 and 1995, did you investigate sniping and shelling incidents in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you investigate cases where so-called modified air bombs hit locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what the investigation procedure was for a sniping or shelling or air bomb incident, and what your role was in an investigation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: As soon as we received word that there had been a sniping attack or artillery attack, my duty was to immediately inform an investigating judge and make sure a team was put together that would inspect the scene. A team was normally made up of a forensic technician, members of the bomb squad, and most of the times there was ballistics expert involved. Once I put together a team, we would go to the crime scene, and once we had assembled there, the judge would distribute our assignments. Sometimes the judge would not be there, and in these cases I would be the one to take over his role. Therefore, my job was, right at the outset, to make sure that the scene was secured by the local police and to make sure that all those who were members of the team did their job properly. Furthermore, my job was to take statements from eye-witnesses, and once all of this was done, I would proceed with writing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In a shelling case, whose job was it to determine the direction of fire of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: That was the job of the bomb squad, and they were the ones who determined the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would they write a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: They would provide information to me or to the judge on the spot about the direction that a missile had come in from. It was at a later stage that they would get any shrapnel or remaining bits of missiles and use these to analyse and eventually compile a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In a sniping case, whose job was it to determine the direction of fire? How would that be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: That depended on how many ballistics experts were available. There weren't too many to go around, to be frank. If none could make it to a scene, then this was normally a job done by one of our forensic experts, who were not properly trained to do that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever have occasion to make a determination of direction of fire in a sniping case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, I did face a situation like that, along with a number of ballistics experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: More on that later. In a sniping case, do you know what kind of information would be relied upon to determine the direction of fire? What sort of factors would be relied upon, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Well, that very much depended on the kind of incident. There were on-site investigations of sniping incidents involving residential buildings. Sometimes these involved residential buildings; sometimes persons were hit out in the street or vehicles. It also depended on the sort of evidence found at a particular crime scene. It was based on all of that that one would determine the direct examination of fire. When dealing with residential buildings, if two different places were found where damage had occurred, based on that, you could determine the direction of fire. Also there were incidents involving vehicles that were hit and damaged. In my investigations, these were usually trams. We needed to locate two different points where damage had occurred, and based on those, we could determine the direction of fire. In addition to any damage we found, we received a lot of assistance from eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show you a document which I'd ask be placed on the ELMO but not broadcast. Actually, if we could pull out a little instead of zooming in because -- yes. Perfect, perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, are we supposed to see that on the ELMO or the e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: ELMO, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document? Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In particular, do you recognise the marking at the bottom in blue pen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I do. That's my signature and the date that I added.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the nine documents which are identified on this spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you the author of many of those documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Indeed, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the document -- those nine documents that you reviewed, were they, to the best of your knowledge, authentic investigative documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Whatever I signed is authentic. The other documents that I saw were not documents that I signed, but they have a familiar form and familiar stamps. They also appear to have been signed by people I knew, people I still know, and I believe those documents to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that this spreadsheet be admitted into evidence under seal, and that the nine documents be admitted into evidence under seal given -- and then can be given separate numbers later. These, of course, have all been made available to Defence counsel. This chart was made available and Defence counsel was aware that we would be employing this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You appear to be anticipating something. But let us hear from Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what Mr. Whiting has just said is true. I did get this list, and we discussed it yesterday, but I think it is an appropriate to draw your attention to the fact that this is a 92 ter witness and his statements were tendered into evidence evidence. On looking at this chart, I have just noticed that two incidents are mentioned, if I'm not mistaken, two incidents which are mentioned in his statement. So according to me, this goes against the provisions of Article 92 ter, to Rule 92 ter, i.e., to discuss matters which are not contained in the statement. The Prosecutor had a choice and had a choice of dealing with these matters in relation to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do have a submission on it, if it's helpful, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll now hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to all of our 92 ter witnesses, we have always in our motion made it clear that we would seek to tender exhibits and documents or relevant documents in through the witness. We have done that with numerous 92 ter witnesses to date, and that's the procedure we're following here. This is -- and I'm doing in the most expeditious, narrow, specific way possible. But this isn't -- this is not inconsistent with how we have been proceeding with respect to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, let me see if I understand your point. You're saying that the 92 ter statement alludes to two incidents, and yet we have an application to admit exhibits that go beyond those two incidents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Five incidents are mentioned in the statement, and these five incidents were included in the list which we were given. But on reviewing the new list we have been given, three incidents have been dropped. One of the incidents is mentioned by the current witness in his statement and only two were kept and then another seven were added on, which the said witness does not mention in his statement, even though he is a 92 ter witness. The incident of the 22nd of December, 1994 is still in there, as well as the incident of the 26th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, if I understand the point being made it is this: Under Rule 92 ter, we're allowed to admit the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement. Now we have that written statement, and that written statement identifies two incidents, or is it five? Well, whatever number it is, the principle is it identifies a number of statements. You seek to have the Chamber admit exhibits that go beyond those incidents mentioned in the statements. So you're seeking to have the Chamber rely on evidence that is strictly not part of the -- of the written statement which we are admitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- this is what we've been doing with every 92 ter witness and we have stated this in every single motion for 92 ter and we've done it with virtually every 92 ter witness that we put in the -- and that is why we have the 30 minutes, or even more time, if it's necessary, but 30 minutes to seek clarifications in the statement but also to put in relevant exhibits, relevant documents that can go into evidence through the witness. And so with respect to these 92 ter witnesses, they are always -- it's the statement that goes in and then we always put in exhibits, and these exhibits are both relevant to the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the abbreviation doesn't relate to the statement. It is to the procedure in court. So the statement which you seek to have admitted should be as full as possible, as comprehensive as possible as to the evidence that you want to have admitted. When a witness comes to court, there is an abbreviated procedure by which we simply admit the statement, but the point that is being made and which I'd like to you consider over the break is whether as a matter of principle it is proper or permissible to introduce exhibits, the effect of which would be to have the Chamber rely on evidence that is properly not part of the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would say just three things in response to this. First of all, the 92 ter statement is broad enough to capture these documents, because the witness says in his 92 ter statement that he investigated a lot of sniping and shelling incidents and these are some of the -- these are all incidents that he investigated, and there are only nine of them. He does talk specifically about several incidents but he talks about having investigated a lot of sniping and shelling. The second point is, I suppose what we could do is when the witness comes and we've identified the documents and any new information, we could take a new statement of the witness and then have that introduced via 92 ter. There are tremendous logistical difficulties with that which I submit make it almost impossible to do, because the new statement then has to be sworn, it has to then be translated under the Rules, disclosed, and then -- and all of that process within the couple of days during which the witness is here. And so what we're done instead is to just do a very short, abbreviated version in court of this. The Defence knew last week that we were going to use these documents. They had this list of documents, so there's no notice issue. I have narrowed the list. I have dropped some things, but I've not added to it. It's -- they have had the list of exhibits and known what was going to go in since last week, and again, this is a practise that we have followed with each 92 ter witness. I would submit it's the most efficient process and if we cannot put in documents this way, then we're going to have to drop doing 92 ter witness and do them live because these documents are essential to our case, and so I think this is it a fair practice of combining 92 ter with a little bit of life evidence to put in documents. The Defence has plenty of notice. It's a practice we have followed in this case, and it's been followed in many other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in this case you may not have a problem, because, as you say, in the witness's statement he does say: "I investigated in Sarajevo a lot of sniping and shelling." The point that I'm making - and I'm not sure whether you're disagreeing with it - is that the exhibits that you seek to tender through a 92 ter witness should be "terminus" in content with the statement. I believe that must be correct. I don't think they can go beyond. They should not introduce, as it were, new incidents or new evidence or evidence other than that which is referred to in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is so, then, well, a question of notice may arise, although you say that the Defence was notified. But there is also the question of principle as to whether it is in keeping with the provisions of the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, though I think there's nothing in the rule that prohibits us from doing this combined procedure, and I think the rule allows that, it's been done, and we have done it in this case. I do take the Court's point and we will seek to address it. If we think that -- if we intend -- we will try to limit the exhibits to what's in the statement, and if we seek to go beyond that, then we will try to resolve the problem, either by taking a new statement or speaking with the Defence to achieve some resolution. But I do take -- I take that point, but I think in this case the statement -- the documents are narrow, they're within the statement, and they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the spreadsheet that was tendered before our break will be admitted as Exhibit P277 under seal, and the nine documents contained within the spreadsheet will be assigned exhibit numbers out of court which will be announced on Tuesday morning, and those will also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I did not feel -- according to what you said, I did not understand that this list with that document was actually tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did tender the list, and the reason I did so is because the witness testified about it. In order to make a complete record and to understand how the things fit together and to confirm that he said these documents are authentic, you need to have the list into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit the list. Based on the discussion that we had prior to the break, we will admit the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just have a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You are still leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you have occasion to investigate a sniping on a tram where the investigation included looking through the sniping holes with tubes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once, by applying this method, along with ballistic experts, we attempted to determine the direction of the shot. We put the tube by fixing two damages caused by the projectile and thereby we established the approximate, or, rather, we established the direction from which the shot had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you one or two questions about that in a moment. But before I do, did you ever face any difficulties when you were investigating sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to be more specific about what difficulties you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, was there ever any -- when you went to a scene where a sniping had occurred, was there ever any problem that you faced to go to the specific spot where the sniping had occurred? Was that ever impeded or made difficult in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Well, from the moment we arrived at the scene, there was danger, both on the way to the specific location where we were supposed to do the on-site investigation, coming from fire from any kind of weapon. So at all times that was a problem. At the very scene, while we were conducting the investigation in the incident with the tram that you mentioned, it was risky to perform our procedures in the way we did. There was always a possibility for this location to be fired at again, the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, excuse me one minute. [Interpretation] Witness, please, before the break, when asked by the Prosecutor who was determining where the shots came from in the sniping incidents, you answered by saying that you were calling on ballistic experts; and when they weren't available, you called on the members of your own team. You talked about these ballistic experts once again. So this is my question: I would like to know first whether those ballistic experts belonged to your own police services or to other police service, whether they belonged to the army, for example. And secondly, whether your mission, the mission of your team with the -- the mission that you had as well as the ballistic experts were interchangeable. You said that when ballistic experts were not available, you were able to determine where the shots came from, which is essential for us, of course, to know where these shots came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking about all these people that I mentioned being part of the team conducting investigations, we were solely members of the civilian police. There were never any members of the military or any other organisation with us. As for the fact that was mentioned when it was impossible for a ballistics expert to visit the scene, our technicians, who were trained to do that, were able to establish the direction of fire. My role was to attend the investigation and to compile an Official Note to be sent afterwards to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look, please, at 65 ter 2825; it's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I'm wrong, but on the list I was given, I cannot find this photograph. I can't find the 65 ter number. It's 2825; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I communicated a list last week of all the documents I would use with the witness, and in that -- when I communicated the list, I said in addition we would notify Defence counsel of any maps or photographs that we would use. I then sent an e-mail to counsel, I believe it's two days ago - I could find it - in which I conveyed the additional information that this witness would talk about with respect to this photograph, and I said that we would use this photograph -- he would mark it on this photograph. So notice has been provided that I would use this photograph for that specific purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, in principle, that should have been notified at the same time, when you sent in the photograph -- when you sent in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I sent in the list long before I had even met with the witness and so I didn't even know about this incident. And it was sent -- the additional information was sent -- excuse me, I believe well before the deadline . I think it's well -- well before 48 hours. So I think it satisfies the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Isailovic, your case manager says that she hasn't received it? Is she saying that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, I looked and it was not on the list, but if this is this photograph that we're very familiar with now, we can see it on the screen. It is a shot of Sarajevo, I believe, so I think it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us view the well-viewed photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the -- you were speaking a moment ago about the investigation of the tram incident. Is the location where the tram was fired on shown on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, with the assistance of the usher, that you mark where the tram was fired on with a circle and then mark with a line where you determine the firing to have come from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The tram was approximately here, and the shot came from this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could that photograph be saved and admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now please see 65 ter 877A. This is one of the documents that has been admitted into evidence. It's a report of the witness. And if it could please not be broadcast. And if we could have page 1 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you just take a moment to look at this document, and do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would draw your attention to the last paragraph on the page you are looking at in B/C/S, and in English it is the middle paragraph that starts with: "Following the examination of the scene ..." There's information there about the direction of fire. Can you recall how it was determined, the direction of fire, in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The direction was established based on the damage caused by the projectile, the penetrating projectile through the window which had a plastic sheet on it, and at the other end there was damage caused by the same projectile in the curtains. So we had two reference points that we were able to connect and, in that way, establish the direction from which this shot had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the windows of this apartment building faced which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: They were facing the part of the neighbourhood where the Bosnian Serb positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall if you learned during this investigation if there was any fighting going on at the time, any combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I believe that it was night-time when this incident happened. We had no reports about any combat operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As a general matter, did you -- do you recall incidents where civilians were killed by snipers during combat activity, while there was combat activity or military fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I cannot remember any such incident, given that during combat operations civilians, for the most part, took cover or shelter in order to avoid being exposed to shooting. Therefore, as far as I was involved, there was not a single sniping incident that took place in the course of a combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic, how much time do you plan to spend in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this witness's statements are now part of the file and of the evidence accepted here, I have to take some time to ask about the incidents that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me how much time, and you must be prepared to do that so the Trial Chamber will make a determination on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a bit difficult for me to assess the time I need. I believe about two hours. About two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, you must focus your cross-examination, Ms. Isailovic. We'll give you an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic; I'm an attorney-at-law with the Paris Bar, and I represent the interests of General Milosevic, the accused in these proceedings. Before coming to The Hague, you took a look at the statements that were given on February 22nd, 1996, and March 11, 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In these statements, you were talking about five incidents. The shelling of the flea market in Bascarsija on December 22nd, 1994. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then you talk about the shelling at Markale on August 28th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The air bomb that fell on the TV building on June 28th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The air bomb that fell on May 26th; in your statement there is no date. Do you remember that it was Safeta Hadzica Street in Srakino Selo. Do you remember what date this occurred, this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1995. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you are also mentioning an incident that occurred on June 28, on Geteova Street at number 5, in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, in these investigating teams, if I understood you right, your role was to come up with a summary report. That's what we would call it in France.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in this report there is a summary of all that has been done by the different members in the investigating team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then, when the job is finished, you would hand over your summary report to the security services centre in Sarajevo, who then drafted what we would call the complaint, the actual legal criminal complaint, "krivicna prijava," in your own language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes. My report was an integral part of this criminal report or criminal charges, along with all other reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you right, in B/C/S you said that this was in addition to the criminal report and to the criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at the end of everything, we see the name Enes Bezdrob as the person who signed those criminal reports, the criminal reports that were drafted after your investigations. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes. He was a chief of the centre and under the law he was the only person authorised to sign criminal reports to be forwarded to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you right, this security services centre in Sarajevo was the central body in Sarajevo and the only entity able to go to the prosecutor, engage the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: For this type of incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're saying for this kind of incident. Could you explain to us what kind of -- type of incidents would actually fall into that category, where there was a need to go through the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Those were mostly criminal offences committed against life and limb and which carried sentences of imprisonment exceeding five years. As for other criminal offences against property, and minor offences, such charges could have been submitted and filed by local police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But this is my question: This summary report that you drafted was not sufficient to seize the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: No, not only on the basis of my report. There were other reports as well, of the people involved in the investigation, and it was up to the Prosecutor to assess whether there were enough elements to proceed with prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the time of reference, 1994/1995, you always applied the Criminal Code that was valid in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I guess that you have legal competencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, but I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
