utterances.text: Within your team, I'm sure -- was there someone who was a legal expert and who was able to explain what the stipulations of the Criminal Code were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The team was led by an investigating judge, and that person was a lawyer by profession, and he or she was the one who assigned tasks to us be carried out at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you right, you said earlier that the -- that the investigating judge did not always take part in the investigation, and in such a case you would step in and replace him. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So my -- I have a question on those occasions where he wasn't there. I believe that within your team there must have been someone with some legal capacities that could -- that would know of the Criminal Code and its provisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I stood in for him. I was versed in the criminal law provisions, and it was my duty to abide by those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your training is, what your background is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: High school or administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If this gets too specific, I think we need to go into private session, if we're going to talk specifically about training and background. If it gets specific and could identify, it's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you're going to proceed along those lines, I agree, because we have to be careful about identifying the witness. Are you going to follow that line?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't mind if we move to something else. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. The interpreter apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind going into private session, because I do want to establish what the background of the witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session. Let's move on

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just resume. In other words, you were the person who was controlling the work conducted by the local police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, but only from the moment I arrived at a given crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I can reasonably conclude that you arrived when the local police had already started investigating the site; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The local police never started the investigation. They just secured the scene, and we would normally come as soon as we received their call. They would guard the crime scene until our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, therefore, every time you reached a site, potential evidence to be recovered from that site had not been investigated by anyone yet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I don't know what could have been going on before we arrived. It really depends on the incident; right? Something could have been tampered with. In this way, for example, some people were killed, some people were injured, so they were taken away from the actual scene to hospital to be helped. It is possible that whatever movable items had been found at the scene were eventually moved. My job was to talk to the scene-of-crime officers and try to ascertain with anything had been tampered with, changed or moved prior to our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your summary reports, did you include any of these observations, i.e., namely, whether the offence or crime had been committed in another spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: If we received that sort of information, we would certainly record it. Otherwise, the only thing that would be included in a report was what we found at a crime scene when we came there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that it was the local police who was, so to speak, in charge of the crime scenes before you actually reached them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: They were the closest to wherever the incident occurred. Their duty was to go there as soon as possible and try to secure it, to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, if I have understood you correctly, your reports are being drafted once you reach the place but do not report anything that happened between the moment the crime was committed and the time you reached the site; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. That misstates the evidence. The witness clearly stated just the opposite. It's at line 12 to 13 of page 52. At least that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At line 12 he says: "If we received that sort of information, we would certainly record it. Otherwise, the only thing that would be included in a report was what we found at a crime scene when we came there."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting this question to you because, on reading your reports, I realised that you did not do, for instance, what one typically does when a crime has been committed; namely, to plot with a piece of chalk where the bodies were located. I have never noticed this in any of your reports or sketches, in any of the photographs which we have had the opportunity to see. Am I right in saying that you have never done this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I wrote the reports. As for the sketches and photographs, this was the job of forensic officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you were preparing a summary report, and I'm sure you had an opportunity to see the appendices that were attached. In other words, in these you could find all the photographs. I'm putting this question to you because you were an eye-witness to all of this: The location of the bodies, of the wounded, found on the crime scene, was this location ever marked, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Normally we found no wounded persons or dead bodies once we arrived at a scene. They would normally be taken away before we arrived. So what we would typically do is mark any points of impact where missiles had exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that 40 or so bodies and 100 wounded people, if we are to evacuate these people, that takes at least an hour and could even take several hours? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for pure speculation. I mean, it depends on how many people are evacuating, under what circumstances. It's purely a speculative kind of question. I don't see how it could possibly be answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Ask another question, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, according to what you know, it takes a while to evacuate the victims and the bodies from the crime scene. Notwithstanding the number, it takes as while, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. It's the same question just rephrased. And it's even more vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. This time she's asking him whether it takes a while, which I presume means that sometimes it takes a while to evacuate the victims and their bodies from the crime scene. Notwithstanding the number, it takes some time. And I feel that I am of the view that the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It certainly takes some time. The question is how long, and I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in all these reports that the Prosecutor has shown you, do any of the reports mention the fact that you arrived on time and actually saw the victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I think there's only this one incident where we found a body, but I'm no longer positive. For the most part, the bodies would be removed. Those wounded would be taken to a hospital to receive assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that all the artifacts you found were put under seal; namely, everything you found on the crime scenes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The criminal procedure provides for the fact that anything found on the crime scene should be put under seal. Are you familiar with this provision of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, as long as we are talking about items and not human bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I talked about artifacts and I was thinking more specifically about projectiles that you may have found on the crime scene. These were put under seal, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes. Bits of projectile, for example, or anything else found at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then the seal is lifted, is it, or ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I can't answer that one. My job was not to guard those items.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. Who in the security services centre is in charge of the custody of these seals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Items from a crime scene would be put away in a warehouse belonging to the forensics department, and once analysis has been conducted they would be stored with the forensic department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the role of an investigating judge, who decided where he was to go and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Investigating judges took the decision themselves. They decided themselves whether they would go to a crime scene or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, part of your duties was to identify the victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And I assume you identified the bodies by picking up the ID cards on the victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: It wasn't just based on that. It really depended on the incident. This normally involved a number of different actions, identifying a body. We got relatives to identify bodies whenever we could, whoever knew the victim, and depending on the condition of the body, sometimes that wasn't possible. Our procedure was decided on a case-to-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. When some people had no ID cards, you drafted something like an ID report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The only thing I did was draw up a record and list anything I found at a site. I also gave grounds for identifying a body. Once our job was done, the actual IDing of a body would be done by my colleagues from a different department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Just a comment I would like to say. An ID report, line 16, I don't know. That doesn't mean a thing to me. I assume it's the same for the Bench. I used a technical word, [Foreign language spoken] -- would be minutes but minutes of an ID, ID report. It's a legal deed, which is mentioned in, I assume, a number of criminal codes. I don't know what translation you got, so I -- sort of "zapisnik" in your language or "identificacija."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: The question I heard was based on an identifying document, an ID card or something like. Whenever an ID card was found, there was no need to compile any further records. This was something that was done later once our work had been done, once we had inspected a site, and I didn't write those. There were other people belonging to a different department doing just that, and the medical expert was also in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. It's -- I'm being technical here. I'd like the interpreters to be careful. In the case of the ID cards -- in the event that the ID card was missing, the minutes or record of identification was then mentioned in the report which you sent off to the public prosecutor. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: What I said is I didn't write those. It was done by police officers belonging to different departments with the assistance of a forensic medical expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we agree on this: The identity of a victim is an essential point when dealing with a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, my question is a very simple one. In your capacity as a person drafting this summary report, did you ever see this ID report or minutes of a person whose ID was not found and in which case it was impossible to prove the person's identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: What I said is this was normally done by police officers belonging to a different department, and they forwarded their reports that were then attached to the criminal report. I didn't have the time or the opportunity to look at their documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you took part in the drafting of the report following what happened on the 28th of August, 1995, the incident on that date. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I wrote my own report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would it not be the case, Witness, that in your report you summarize anything pertaining to the crime allegedly committed at this spot. Is that how you conduct your investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I wrote my report about the incident. We didn't qualify this as a crime. We just wrote a report on what we found at the scene. We tried to describe what we found, what we saw, and possibly what we took from the scene, how we inspected the scene. In addition to my report, you have a report from the on-site investigation that was written up by the investigating judge. So I'm only talking about my own report. It wasn't a report that also included information on what others did or what they found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, the case of this particular incident, here we have documents that have been disclosed to us by the Prosecutor. I assume that these documents pertain to this particular incident. As part of it, we have a list of the victims. This is document 65 ter. The number of the exhibit is 891.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, where is this taking us? What is it that you're trying to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to demonstrate that the reports we have in front of us have been drafted in violation of the -- of criminal law, criminal procedure, and therefore, one would ask for this to be rescinded. This is a legal issue. This has got nothing to do with any kind of suggestion whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If, assuming they are drafted in breach of the domestic legal procedure, would you be going further to contend that on that basis, the information in the report should not be considered by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And why is that? On what evidential or other rule would you be relying for that submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the indictment there is allegation of a number of murders, crimes which have to do with the qualification of crime against humanity. That is an element of crime. If there is no evidence which are legally established, then there is no foundation for the qualification of crime against humanity if we cannot prove the crimes that are -- an element of the crime, and in the interest of justice, I believe that we have to base all the proceedings on legally sound documents. And here we have a witness which was doing more or less a mixed job between that of an instructing magistrate and -- so I'm trying to explain that there are a number of elements that are missing, elements that I believe are absolutely indispensable to establish that an offence had been committed, and a crime even more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are the elements that you say are missing? Because this gentleman was doing a "mixed job." What elements are missing from the crime because of that? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that I'm not well understood because of the translation. I mean, it's not personal, of course, but it is a problem. The identification of victims is part and parcel, is an essential part actually, of establishing the foundation for the commission of an offence. If there's no victim, if there is no person murdered, then there is no crime. And when reading these reports, I was drafting some statistics according to victims, for example, and that noticed that for most of the victims -- I'm not referring here to this incident -- here in this incident I'm not referring to the dead. Of course the dead cannot prove their identity, even though there are ways to do that. But I'm talking about the wounded, the casualties, the wounded. Among the wounded, here we have 65 people, and out of those 65, 20 have an ID card, whereas the others, I don't know. Maybe somewhere there is some kind of -- there is something, but it seems that their identity has not been established, and I believe that it's a prerequisite if you want to have a sound procedure, to establish the identity of the victims. This is why I'm asking the question, because I'm quite curious, I would like to know how the identity of these people was established, people that do not have an identification card, and then there is no identification report that is drawn up after the fact. Of course, sometimes people don't have an ID card, and the witness told us that there is a -- that the identity is actually established, but it's another department that is in charge of that. And I would like to know what -- where we have traces of the work done by this other department, whether we could get them. So I just hope that my meaning was correctly conveyed by the translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your submission is that in the incidents that are alleged in the indictment, the Prosecution must establish the identity of each and every victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that it's the least you can do in a serious investigation, and here we're talking about very serious charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I don't think that's an element of the offence, and in most cases it's not pleaded in the indictment, so I don't -- I would take issue with that view. But perhaps it's not something that will be resolved right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to resolve it, because if I find that it is not pertinent, I will stop this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, certainly with respect to the incident that's been talked about or alluded to, which is shelling number 23, the indictment alleges that 43 persons were killed and 75 were injured. There is no list of specific people who were killed or injured. And I don't think that the elements of the offences that are charged in this case require that the Prosecution prove the specific identity of the person killed. It's just not an element of the offence. We just have to prove that -- if it's murder, you must prove that a person was killed. So I don't see how this question about identity is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has always been my understanding, too. If, for example, Ms. Isailovic, a tram was shot at - and we have evidence that the tram was shot at - and say 15 or 20 persons were injured and five killed, if that were charged, you're saying that to substantiate the charge, the Prosecution must prove the identity of the 15 or 20 injured and the identify of the five who were killed? That's your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily, Your Honour. It depends on accounts against the accused. If we're talking about murder, an act against humanity, then you have to establish that there's been murder, that there's been violence, and to do this I believe that it's absolutely necessary to have a victim. But for other cases using indiscriminatory armed force, then that's not necessarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. I think you have it absolutely right. You must have a victim. The question is, what is the evidence that will satisfy the Chamber that there was a victim in a case like this? That is the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just add that there is a fundamental difference between domestic criminal law and international criminal law in these matters. The offence, as specified in the Statute, is, for instance, indiscriminate attacks, and if you can prove that the attacks were such as to target civilians and military persons indiscriminately, then the case is made. I don't think that the question of identity goes any further than just founding or establishing the fact that someone was killed. And if you're interested, then we can, in some cases, prove the identity of that victim. But it cannot be and it is not a requirement that for these international crimes to be committed you have to identify the identity of each victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, Your Honour, I fully agree with you regarding Article 3, but as far as Article 5 in the Statute, crime against humanity - and maybe this is what you reject - but the elements that are listed in Article 5 must be proved in order for the proceedings to continue and somebody to be found guilty of a crime against humanity. So the main elements of this crime -- and here maybe we're back to the regular Criminal Code. There's murder, which is the case that we have in the indictment, and also violence. But this is qualified in legal terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Let us take murder under Article 5. Let us take murder under Article 5, a crime against humanity. There's a charge of murder of 500 people killed by a bomb. This is a mass crime, and there is evidence from witnesses of the bomb and there is evidence of people being injured by the bomb. Some died as a result of the bomb. Police officers go or other witnesses go to the scene and they can testify that they saw some 500 people there dead immediately after the bomb. We have the names of some; we may not have the names of all. That's enough. Are you saying that in these proceedings we need to identify each and every one of those 500 victims? It's a question of the evidence. You need evidence of a victim, but it will satisfy the Chamber if there is evidence along the lines that I have set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, justly so, I fully agree with you. But we have no one who saw those victims. There are policemen who come after the fact and who draft a report on the crime using statements made by some people, and I believe that the least we could ask for is to verify -- you know, this is it not something that the witness saw, because the witness came after the fact, once everything had been cleaned up. There's no bodies, no wounded. So, I mean, this goes beyond what I know in terms of criminal law, and I do a lot of criminal law. How can it be established in another way? How can you establish what happened in another way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems that you're taking another point then, perhaps, that the crime was not committed or that the bodies were not there or, as your colleague has been suggesting, that they were brought there. That's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know. We're here to establish the facts. I don't want to speculate one way or another. You know, I'm a legal expert; I deal with facts and what I'm interested in are facts. And I believe that is exactly the same for you. I believe it's the only way that we can actually come to the truth, the legal truth; maybe not the material truth but the legal truth. What I want to do is to establish the evidence that will actually prove what really happened, which is why I'm asking that question. Maybe the witness will say that he knows nothing of this, but maybe we can find people who are able to tell us how the identity of all these people was eventually established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: None of it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to think with you and reflect on all this with you, and I believe that your logic is quite relevant. There is no murder; there's no body, there's no victim. And we have to establish the identity, whether the reality of that killing. So I am following you and I'm hearing you. But at the same time, please look at Article 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, (1). In terms of evidence, the Chamber applies the rules that are in this section and is not bound by the domestic rules that have to do with the establishment of evidence. Please read paragraph 89, Rule 89. Because in your logic you are saying that the witness's reports are not correct, as far as you're concerned, because they were not directly sent to the public prosecutor, which should have been done according to the law of the country, but were handed over to his boss, his administrative boss. So this is the question I'm asking: If you are challenging what is in these reports, and if you want the Chamber to disregard them because internal rules were not followed correctly, if that's the basis of the regulations, don't you think that goes against the general provision that I just read to you? Unless you can demonstrate and prove that those reports were fundamentally biased. Because, having been through the hands of the administrative director, there would have been, for example, orders that came from the executive branch to modify them. Are you following me? So you are holding on to the internal rules of country to establish that what the witness has done is not correct, but you're forgetting in the meanwhile the international law and its provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In which case, Ms. Isailovic, if you are saying that the reports were collected in a manner that make them unreliable, then that's a different matter. Are you familiar with Rule 95? Rule 95, that's the rule that is really relevant here. It says: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to, and would seriously damage, the integrity of the proceedings." So if you're going that far, then you should let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judges, this is what I was trying to do with this witness: I was trying to have an opinion on all this, because I was hoping that the witness would tell us about the evidence which I believe are missing in his report. If that's the case and if those additional reports do not exist, then we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me that he has told you as much as he knows. We will adjourn. When I return, I will rule on this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the Chamber has determined that you have spent sufficient time on this issue and you should move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could raise an issue that arose during the break, and I've raised it with Defence counsel. The interpreters have informed me that they have a dispute among themselves about the interpretation of a particular sentence, about what the witness said. One interpreter thinks he said one thing; the other interpreter thinks he said something else. And I shared this with Ms. Isailovic. It relates to the question and answer at page 30 of the transcript, and I think the only way to clear it up is to put the question to him again and ask the witness to clear it up. It's page 30, line 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, line 3. My question was: "In a sniping case, whose job was it to determine the direction of fire? How would that be done?" And the answer the transcript is: "That depended on how many ballistics experts were available. There weren't too many to go around, to be frank. If none could make it to a scene, then this was normally a job done by one of our forensic experts ..." and it's the end of the sentence that's in dispute, "... done by one of our forensic experts who were not properly trained to do that sort of thing." One of the interpreters heard him say "not properly trained" and the other interpreter heard him say that they were properly trained. So it's obviously an important issue, and I wonder if I could just put the question to the witness to ask him to resolve it, if you think that's the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Witness, when I was asking you questions, I asked you this question: In a sniping case, whose job was it to determine the direction of fire? How would that be done. And in your answer, you said: That depended on how many ballistics experts were available. There weren't too many to go around, to be frank. If none could make it to a scene, then this was normally a job done by one of our forensic experts." And then did you say "who were not properly trained to do that sort of thing" or did you say "who were properly trained to do that sort of thing"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before he answers, I think the value of his answer, I think, will be somewhat diminished by the fact that you disclosed, in his presence, the disputed translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's one or the other. I mean the question is what he said. I don't think it's leading in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that our forensic technicians were skilled to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- in any event, if there is any further dispute about it or further question, the Trial Chamber has -- we could also ask to listen again to the original tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I think we should move on. We have spent enough time. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, is it fair to say that when you were drafting the summary reports intended for the public prosecutor, you never consulted the military authorities of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes. We wrote our reports for the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, is this the same line of questioning? Because I've told you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what's happening here. In English, everything is correctly translated, but the witness is talking about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I meant move on to a different topic. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about another topic. I'm still looking at the reports, because here we have a witness that can tell us about the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I would like to know: Before drafting your final summary report, did you consult with the military authorities of the BiH army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: No, I didn't consult them. I wrote my report myself, and whatever is said there is only my product.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, can I infer from this that for you, the military situation between the warring factions in Sarajevo was not an element that you would include in your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: No. The report contained only what I saw with my own eyes and what I found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not take into account whatever military activity had been going on when a crime had occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: No. I was not even familiar with the military activities. We did the job that we were assigned to do, and that was to examine and to see what happened at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, often members of UNPROFOR were part of your investigating team; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes. These were UNPROFOR military observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, in other words, they were with you doing the same job that members of the investigating team would be doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: No. They were present there, but they had no contact with us. They did their part of the job and we did our job. Practically they were simply observing what we were doing, but what they wrote in their reports, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When, in your report, you're saying that such-and-such a member of UNPROFOR was there, it means that he was just there as a mute witness during the investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: It says in the report that they were present there. It does not say that they were members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when writing this final summary report, did you ever take into account any reports that had been drafted by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Provided they told us something relevant or made any comments, we would note it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But earlier, Witness, when talking to the Prosecutor, you talked about a tram incident which occurred on October 8th, 1994; do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This incident occurred on the 8th of October, and the report is dated the 10th of October, 1994. Can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I can't see the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you need to see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, it's 65 ter 641A, and if it could not be broadcast. Just to be clear, I don't believe I asked any questions about this incident. The report was put in, but the incident that I asked about and he marked the map about was not this incident, that he marked the photograph about. Just so that it's clear, because there is some reference to the fact that I had asked him questions about it. But just so there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you see the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you don't mention any military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I really apologise. In this case it is not his report, the report is not from him, so it misstates the evidence. He is present, but it's not his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecutor is right. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Your name here is mentioned. It's the third name on the list. You are one of the members investigating the case; is that right? And as you took part in this, did you ever address the question of military activities between you, those military activities that occurred on the 8th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: I can't remember many details. I didn't write this report; therefore, I don't know if my colleague took that into account or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document, which is 00-0918. It's a letter sent to the warring parties by General Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Remove it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he have anything to do with the letter sent to the warring parties by General Rose? Is there anything in it on which he can testify?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's just it. I'm wanting to show the witness that there were military activities that are not recorded in the report, and to my mind this is important. Precisely, General Rose addresses this to the two warring parties who were the cause of the shooting, because this relates to the incident that occurred on the 8th of October, which is what is being discussed right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what he has to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of these military activities that occurred on the 8th of October and that led to this correspondence between Mr. Ganic, Izetbegovic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-28
utterances.text: As I said before, I didn't know about any planned military activities that were in progress. This letter is in English and I can't read English; therefore, I don't know what it says or where the military activities actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have read the letter quickly - it's a little hard to read - but I don't see a reference to the military activity on the 8th of October. Maybe I'm missing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the section of the report to which you wish to draw the witness's attention and that you say is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 3, I'm sorry, because we're now on page 2. "Our right to protest ..." -- this is addressed to Mr. Izetbegovic. It's dated the 9th of October, General Rose, it says: "I want to protest in the strongest possible terms about sniping incidents that took place on the 8th of October, 1994, in the city of Sarajevo from both sides of the line of confrontation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you wish to ask the witness whether he knows anything about those sniping incidents that took place on the 8th of October? What's your answer to that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'm not sure what time on the 8th of October. Is this in reference to the incident that I witnessed? Nevertheless, I am not familiar with this letter; I have never set eyes on it. And, as I said, I was not aware of any other activities in any other places across Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we have an exhibit number for this document marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no objection. I'm happy to have this letter exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarification, there was a photo marked yesterday by Witness Jordan that was mistakenly tendered and admitted twice as Exhibit D79 and Exhibit D80. That will retain the exhibit number Exhibit D79, and this will be admitted as Exhibit D80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you took part in and even signed the report which is exhibit -- 65 ter number 665. On page 2 --?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should consider issues of protection here. The name might crop up, so maybe we should do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: My name is Ziba Subo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: 1947, 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember at the beginning of April 1995 giving a statement to the Bosnian police authorities about what happened to you, your family and your cousin Mrs. Custovic, on 7 April 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I remember. I don't forget things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have ter number 00012E on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have your reading glasses on, Mrs. Subo?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that appears on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that your statement from 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the first exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you also recall giving a statement to the ICTY in November 1995 about the same incident, at which time I was present?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I now have ter number 02964 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while waiting for that, perhaps I could ask you, Mrs. Subo, in preparing to testify here, were both of these statements read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you have any changes or corrections to make to them at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't change anything. Everything remains as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document appears on the screen in front of you now, Mrs. Subo?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that your statement from November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Next, if I could have two photographs in succession, 00012B and, following that, 00012D, please. Can you magnify the photograph. Can you magnify it further for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Subo, do you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, and I will never forget it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you recognise it, perhaps you could tell the Trial Chamber what you recognise, then.

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I recognise everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What is it, Mrs. Subo?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: This is where the family house crumbled down and this is where my cousin was killed and this was where I was with my family. That's our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what I understand you're telling the Trial Chamber is this is your house after it was hit by the bomb on 7 April 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is, at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can we move to the next and final photograph. I think you might have to make it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the next photograph on the screen in front of you, Mrs. Subo?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember this well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: It's a ruin that fell on top of me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this the ruin of your house after it was hit by the bomb, Mrs. Subo?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: When the bomb flattened it, yes. This is how it remained in both photographs, the first one and this one. Flattened, razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Subo, I just have some very short questions for you. In your statement in 1995, November 1995, you mentioned that there was some kind of military structure about ten minutes' walk from your house but you didn't know what it was. Do you know now what that military structure might have been?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I don't know. I still don't. It might have been a kitchen or something like that, military, with a -- but I try not to think about it, because on the 7th of April, in Foca, my house was destroyed the same way as this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the time leading up to the attack on your house, do you recall ever seeing any soldiers in the immediate area?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: There was a war on. There were soldiers around; I don't know who or why, or what soldiers, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the immediate area, do you recall seeing any of those soldiers engaged in military activity? In other words, did you see any shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. I was a housewife. I never left the house. I wasn't supposed to leave the house, didn't have the courage. I don't know anything about that. The only thing I do know about is what befell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see any mortars?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness has answered that question and said that she didn't see anything, so I don't see any point in continuing. We're only wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. I have concluded the questioning in chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Mrs. Branislava Isailovic; I'm a member of the Paris Bar Association. I shall ask you a few questions concerning this incident in which you were a witness and a victim. This occurred on the 7th of April, 1995. On the screen a moment ago we saw the statement that you made, that you gave to the police; is that right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was presented by the Prosecution. This was number 12. This is a 65 ter document. If we could see it on the screen, please. If Ms. Edgerton could help me find the page of the statement so that we can speed things up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 12E. That's not it. 00012E. Isn't that what -- we're asking for the 65 ter number, 00012E.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the same statement as the one we've seen a few minutes ago. I would like to draw your attention to this last long paragraph. Could you read it. It starts there, "... who took me to the hospital. In the meantime, I told a young man by the name of Zijo that my sister Ziba Custovic, with her daughter Aldijana, was in one of the rooms, and to please search these in order to find them, find her alive or dead."

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes. She was found dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the truth, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Yes. When I escaped from the rubble, I went over and that's the last thing I remember. I only know that I ended up seeing my family again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can I infer that after seeing the rubble around your house you did not see your sister again?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: I saw her when I escaped from the ruin. I glanced back. I saw a head cut in half. I don't know what happened later. Maybe I fell down. The next thing I remember is the hospital. I know she was dead. I know that this was a serious misfortune, a heavy blow, but that's all I remember. I don't know what else to say. It's all there in the photographs for to you to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I mean. There is a slight discrepancy with your statement. What you're saying today is that you saw her or you didn't see her? Because in the statement it says that. In your statement which we have just seen, you state that you heard no noise; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: No, no noise whatsoever. I just went there to get some coffee to brew. I know that I was enveloped by darkness. There was shooting before that and then I hurried off to the basement with my children and then I was enveloped by darkness. I felt an impact; I felt objects smashing against me and I realised that something must have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. One last question which has to do with military presence in Hrasnica. Were you accustomed to seeing soldiers in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIBA SUBO
utterances.text: Well, they sometimes passed through. Who knows where they were going. They all had uniforms. I didn't know if it was a soldier or just somebody wearing a uniform. I don't know much about these things. I only know about my own problems. I didn't care about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave. We'll adjourn until Tuesday, 2.15, and the first matter we'll take up -- let's move into private session. Well, may we have the witness leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.11 p.m.,
